Four traps in raw text that change a count

Before you count

Sheets counts the exact letters you type. Raw text has four traps that make a count too big or too small.

  • 1 · One idea, many words
  • 2 · Caption junk
  • 3 · One loud video
  • 4 · Editing the evidence

Trap 1 · One idea, many words

People say the same thing in different ways.

  • Variants. "break" also catches "breaks". Helpful. But on YouTube "rate" shows up in 6 chunks, some of them "separate", "hydrated" and "corporate".
  • Synonyms. The Time Off Task video says "idle time" in 5 chunks and "time off task" in only 1.

  • You want to count talk about area managers. What do you type?

Matching isn't case sensitive: "Pay", "pay" and "PAY" count the same.

Trap 2 · Caption junk

YouTube captions are machine-made. They add tags nobody chose to say.

  • [Music]
    in 9 chunks
  • [ __ ] a bleeped swear word
    in 19 chunks, 17 of them from one video

  • Should [Music] go on your phrase list?

Trap 3 · One loud video

Each review is a different person. YouTube's 98 chunks come from just 8 videos.

"peak season" appears in 12 YouTube chunks. Each square is one chunk; the marked ones come from the same video.

Trap 4 · Editing the evidence

Never edit the text column. It's your evidence.

You'll quote it in your brief, and the AI tool needs the full wording in Step 3. Small words carry meaning: "no breaks" is a complaint, "breaks" alone might not be.

How to count by video. On the YouTube tab, click Data → Create a filter. On column E (text), choose Filter by condition → Text contains and type your phrase. Read the title column of the rows that stay.

Three things to remember

Pick your words with the traps in mind.

  • Pick the right versionList variants and synonyms. Count the version that catches real mentions.
  • Skip caption tags[Music] and [ __ ] aren't topics.
  • Count YouTube by videoIf one video gives most of a count, call it one worker's story.
